newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn hopes Ankara softens tone over fatal fire.
newsitem.headline: Bonn hopes Ankara softens tone over fatal fire.

text.p: Germany said on Friday it hoped strained relations with Turkey would improve after police indicated that a fire in which a Turkish woman and two of her children died was not the result of a racist attack.
The dead woman's 42-year-old husband was remanded in custody on suspicion of starting the fire in the town of Krefeld on Sunday night, a police detective told reporters.

Turkey's Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, had angered Germany by blaming the attack, together with a suspected racist firebombing in the Netherlands in which six Turks died, on rising anti-Moslem sentiment in the West.

"It looks like it wasn't a racist attack. I just hope that we can get moderation and restraint from Turkey that we haven't had up to now," German government spokesman Herbert Schmuelling told a news conference.
Several hundred people attended a memorial ceremony for the victims in a hall in Cologne where rival Kurdish and Turkish groups chanted and waved banners.

Turkish ambassador Volkan Vural was jeered by the crowd, some of whom blamed Turkey for the deaths, and there were scuffles as a young man tried to drape a Kurdish flag over the coffin of one of the victims.
Police had said all along they believed the fire was started deliberately, but that there was no evidence of a racist attack.
Walter Seifert, the head of Krefeld's murder squad, said an eyewitness had seen the suspect filling a canister with petrol at a filling station.

Seifert said investigations indicated that the suspect had regularly beaten his wife and children and brought a prostitute to live in the apartment for a time. He said the wife had planned to sue for divorce in the next few days.

The wife was fatally injured when she jumped from their third-floor in the town centre. A 16-year-old daughter died in hospital from injuries and a 17-year-old son was found dead in the building. Two other daughters also jumped from the flat and were severely injured.

Erbakan's comments had fuelled a war of words between Turkey and Germany, which is particularly sensitive to such accusations that it is soft on racism after working hard to quell an upsurge of anti-foreigner attacks after unification in 1990.
More than 30 people died then, among them five Turkish women and children in a single attack in Solingen in 1993.

Some German commentators have attributed Turkey's response to fears, stoked by comments from European conservatives at a recent congress, that it is being shut out of European integration because it does not have a Christian culture.

A leading Bonn parliamentarian, Christian Democrat parliamentary business manager Joachim Hoerster, said that what he called "unbelievable gaffes" by Turkish officials would make it harder for Turkey to join the European Union.
"Mr Erbakan must realise that Europe is bigger than eastern Anatolia," he said.
